sections.h: How the Song is built and how it has been read
sections.b:
The Song is eight chapters of poems in two main voices, a woman and a man, with a chorus called the 'daughters of Jerusalem'. Scholars divide it differently: Michael Fox counts thirty-one separate poems, others find one poem built round the oath (2:7; 3:5; 8:4) and the refrain 'my lover belongs to me and I belong to him' (2:16; 6:3; 7:10). Four main ways of reading it exist, often combined: allegory (God and Israel, Christ and the Church, the soul and God); love poetry about human love; a drama with two or three characters; and a wedding or festival liturgy.

Most modern scholars read it as love poetry. Most Jewish and Christian readers before about 1800 read it as allegory, and the allegory still shapes Jewish and Catholic teaching. The Plain translates the Hebrew without choosing between them, and the notes give each reading.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 1:1; Song of Songs 2:7; Song of Songs 2:16; Song of Songs 3:5; Song of Songs 6:3; Song of Songs 7:10; Song of Songs 8:4

common: Most modern scholars read the Song as love poetry about a man and a woman.
uncommon: A few scholars read the Song as a collection of lines from a cult of sacred marriage (Pope on the Mesopotamian parallels), a view most reject.

claude.title: The Song's silence about God
claude.body: The Song has no divine name apart from the debated 'flame of Yah' (8:6) and no word of covenant, law or temple. I suggest this silence is part of the book's argument: it says that human love is worth a whole book without being turned into something else. Each reading handles the silence in its own way: the allegories fill it, the love-poetry reading leaves it, and the wisdom reading says that God's gifts are enjoyed in the world he made. The idea overlaps with much published comment on the book's wisdom setting (Fox, Murphy, Davis).

sections.h: Solomon in the Song of Songs
sections.b: Solomon is named seven times in the Song (1:1, 5; 3:7, 9, 11; 8:11, 12). In the title he is the book's patron, and 1 Kings 4:32 says he wrote 1,005 songs. In 3:6–11 he is the king in the litter on his wedding day. In 8:11–12 the woman sets her own vineyard against his and tells him he may keep his thousand. Readers differ on whether he is the lover, a stock figure of royal love, or a foil to the shepherd lover. The Song says nothing of his wisdom, his temple or his many wives, though 6:8 counts a royal harem.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 1:1; Song of Songs 3:7–11; Song of Songs 6:8; Song of Songs 8:11–12; 1 Kings 4:32; 1 Kings 11:1–3

common: The title ties the Song to Solomon, but most scholars think the poems were gathered later.

sections.h: Marriage in the Song of Songs
sections.b: The Song does not mention a wedding contract, a dowry or children. It speaks of a mother's house (3:4; 8:2), of brothers who control a girl's future (1:6; 8:8–9), of a wedding day for a king (3:11), and of 'my sister, my bride' (4:9–5:1). Its lovers are free to say 'I belong to my lover and my lover belongs to me' (2:16; 6:3). Christian and Jewish teachers have used the Song both to praise marital love and to say what it is for. The card at 7:10 sets out the churches' differing answers.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 3:4; Song of Songs 3:11; Song of Songs 4:9; Song of Songs 5:1; Song of Songs 8:8–10

sections.h: The bride in the Song and in later reading
sections.b: The word kallah, 'bride', appears first in 4:8 and is repeated through 5:1. The Song gives the bride a voice and a name of her own ('the Shulammite', 6:13). Jewish readers took her as Israel (Targum, Rashi); Christians as the Church (Cyprian, Ambrose) or the soul (Origen, Bernard, John of the Cross). The bride and lover of the Song lie behind the Friday-evening hymn Lekha Dodi, written at Safed in the 1500s to welcome the Sabbath as a bride. The Song is not quoted in the New Testament's bridal passages, which draw on the prophets.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 4:8–5:1; Song of Songs 6:13; Isaiah 62:5; Ephesians 5:25–32; Revelation 19:7–9

sections.h: Wine and love in the Song of Songs
sections.b: Wine is the Song's measure of love. Love is 'better than wine' (1:2, 4; 4:10); the woman offers spiced wine and pomegranate juice (8:2); the lover drinks his wine with his milk (5:1); a mouth is like the best wine (7:9). The 'house of wine' (2:4) is the banquet hall. The Song does not condemn wine and does not tell the reader to drink. It uses wine as a picture of pleasure that is sweet, strong and shared, as Proverbs 5:19 does for love in marriage.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 1:2; Song of Songs 2:4; Song of Songs 4:10; Song of Songs 5:1; Song of Songs 7:9; Song of Songs 8:2; Proverbs 5:19

sections.h: Vineyards in the Song of Songs
sections.b: The vineyard is the Song's picture of the woman and of love's ownership. She says she guarded her brothers' vineyards but not her own (1:6). Foxes ruin the vineyards in bloom (2:15). Her lover pastures among the vineyards of En-gedi (1:14). The book ends with two vineyards: Solomon's at Baal-hamon, rented for a thousand pieces of silver, and 'my own vineyard' that she keeps (8:11–12). Isaiah 5:1–7 sings a love song of a vineyard that stands for Israel, and Jewish and Christian readers have heard that song behind the Song's.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 1:6; Song of Songs 1:14; Song of Songs 2:15; Song of Songs 8:11–12; Isaiah 5:1–7

sections.h: The mountain of myrrh and frankincense
sections.b: In the Song, frankincense and myrrh are the scents of the garden and the bed (3:6; 4:6, 14). The lover goes 'to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense' (4:6), a place that Jewish readers took as Mount Moriah and the Temple, where incense burned (Exodus 30:34–38), and Christian readers as Calvary. In the plain sense it is the woman's body, as 'the mountains of spices' (8:14) is.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 3:6; Song of Songs 4:6; Song of Songs 4:14; Song of Songs 8:14; Exodus 30:34–38

sections.h: Sheba's spices and the Song
sections.b: Sheba, in southern Arabia, was the source of frankincense and myrrh, the two scents most named in the Song (1 Kings 10:2, 10; Isaiah 60:6). The Song's list of spices (4:14), with nard from the Himalayas and cinnamon from the east, shows the trade routes that served Solomon's court. Origen made a link between the dark woman of 1:5 and the queen of Sheba, which the text does not say.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 1:5; Song of Songs 3:6; Song of Songs 4:14; 1 Kings 10:2; 1 Kings 10:10; Isaiah 60:6

sections.h: Gold and stones in the man's praise
sections.b: The wasf of the lover (5:10–16) is made of gold, ivory, 'stones from Tarshish', sapphires (lapis lazuli) and marble on bases of gold. The woman's jewelry is gold with silver dots (1:10–11). Solomon's litter is silver, gold and purple (3:10). The materials are those of the temple and the royal court, and the effect is of a lover seen as a work of art.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 1:10–11; Song of Songs 3:10; Song of Songs 5:11–15; Exodus 28:20

sections.h: Types in the Song of Songs
sections.b: The Song is not quoted in the New Testament, and the old typological readings (Christ the bridegroom, the Church the bride, Mary the garden) come from the early church's habit of reading all Scripture in the light of Christ, not from any New Testament use. Jewish readers had their own: the lover is God at the Exodus and Sinai, the bride is Israel, the garden is the Land. Modern readers differ on whether the typological sense is part of what the text means or a later use of it. See the allegorical-reading page.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 2:8–14; Song of Songs 4:12; Song of Songs 6:9; Ephesians 5:31–32

sections.h: The Song of Songs and the canon
sections.b: The Mishnah reports that Rabbi Akiva called the Song the holy of holies and that its status was questioned by some (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5). The Tosefta forbids singing it in banquet houses (Tosefta Sanhedrin 12:10). Avot de-Rabbi Natan (version A, chapter 1) lists it among books once considered for withdrawal. Origen reports a rule among Jews of his time that the Song should not be read by the young. In the Christian church its place was not disputed, though Theodore of Mopsuestia is reported to have rejected the allegorical reading and Sebastian Castellio (1544) to have called it lascivious. The Song is one of the five Scrolls (Megillot) of the Jewish Writings, read at Passover.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 1:1; Song of Songs 8:6–7

sections.h: The Song and the single life
sections.b: The Song speaks to the unmarried in three ways: the oath not to wake love before it wants (2:7; 3:5; 8:4), the brothers' watch over a young sister (8:8–9), and the night search that ends with the woman beaten (5:7). Monastic readers took the Song as the voice of the soul wedded to Christ (Origen, Bernard, John of the Cross, Teresa of Ávila), and the Orthodox and Catholic traditions honor vowed virginity beside marriage. Protestant teachers use the oath as a call to wait until marriage. The cards at 7:10 and 8:8 set the answers out.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 2:7; Song of Songs 3:5; Song of Songs 5:7; Song of Songs 8:4; Song of Songs 8:8–10

sections.h: Egyptian and Mesopotamian love songs
sections.b: The Song shares much with the love songs of Egypt (Papyrus Chester Beatty I, the Turin papyrus, Papyrus Harris 500, the Cairo Love Songs) and with Sumerian songs of Dumuzi and Inanna: lovers called 'sister' and 'brother', love as sickness, gardens and perfumes, the lover at the door. Michael Fox's study (1985) is the standard comparison. The likenesses show a common tradition, not a copy, and the Song has neither gods nor rites. Greek pastoral poetry (Theocritus) is a later comparison.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 2:5; Song of Songs 4:9; Song of Songs 5:2–6; Song of Songs 4:12

sections.h: Eden echoes in the Song of Songs
sections.b: The Song's garden is full of the first garden's elements: a spring (4:12, 15), fruit trees, spices, a man and woman who are not ashamed. It uses a word for the 'breezy part of the day' close to Genesis 3:8 (2:17; 4:6) and the word for desire from Genesis 3:16 (7:10). Phyllis Trible read the Song as a return to Eden's harmony. The locked garden (4:12) opened by the woman (4:16) answers the gate closed in Genesis 3:24. Not all scholars find these echoes deliberate.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 2:17; Song of Songs 4:6; Song of Songs 4:12–16; Song of Songs 7:10; Genesis 2:8–25; Genesis 3:8; Genesis 3:16

sections.h: The Song of Songs as a Marian text
sections.b: The Song became a Marian text in the Latin church from about the fourth century. The Vulgate's Tota pulchra es, amica mea (4:7), Quae est ista quae ascendit (3:6; 8:5), Hortus conclusus (4:12) and pulchra ut luna (6:10) are sung on Marian feasts, notably the Immaculate Conception and the Assumption. The East also uses the garden and spring images for the Mother of God. Protestant churches do not apply the Song to Mary. The cards at 4:12 and 8:5 set out the views.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 3:6; Song of Songs 4:7; Song of Songs 4:12; Song of Songs 6:10; Song of Songs 8:5

sections.h: The Song among the wisdom books
sections.b: The Song is counted among the Writings with Proverbs and Ecclesiastes and is attributed, like them, to Solomon. Its themes touch both: the praise of the wife of one's youth (Proverbs 5:15–20), the foreign woman's perfumed bed (Proverbs 7:17–18), enjoying life with the wife one loves (Ecclesiastes 9:9). Some scholars argue the Song belongs to wisdom literature as a poem about one of life's great goods (Murphy, Davis). Wisdom of Solomon 8:2 speaks of wooing Wisdom as a bride, a different book with a related image.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 1:1; Proverbs 5:15–20; Proverbs 7:17–18; Ecclesiastes 9:9

sections.h: Love strong as death, jealousy hard as Sheol
sections.b: Song of Songs 8:6 compares love to death and jealousy to Sheol, the two powers that take all and let go of nothing. The comparison does not say love is stronger than death; Christian readers sometimes hear that in it because of the resurrection. Elsewhere Sheol is the place that is never satisfied (Proverbs 30:15–16) and whose grip no one can escape (Psalm 49:7–9).
sections.refs: Song of Songs 8:6; Proverbs 30:15–16; Psalm 49:7–9

sections.h: Genesis 3:16 and Song of Songs 7:10
sections.b: The Hebrew word teshuqah ('desire') occurs three times: Genesis 3:16 (the woman's desire for her husband), Genesis 4:7 (sin's desire for Cain) and Song of Songs 7:10 (the man's desire for the woman). Phyllis Trible argued that the Song's use undoes the curse of Genesis 3:16. Others find the echo too slight. The Greek of Genesis has 'turning away' (apostrophē) in both places, and the Greek of the Song has 'turning' (epistrophē).
sections.refs: Genesis 3:16; Genesis 4:7; Song of Songs 7:10

sections.h: Yah in Song of Songs 8:6
sections.b: The Song never uses the LORD (YHWH) or the title God. The one possible exception is shalhevetyah in 8:6, which can be read 'a flame of Yah' (the short form of the LORD's name, as in Exodus 15:2) or as an intensive, 'a mighty flame', as in Jonah 3:3. The Greek and Latin have no divine name there. If Yah is the name, it is the only place in the book that names God.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 8:6; Exodus 15:2; Jonah 3:3

sections.h: The seal on the heart (Song of Songs 8:6)
sections.b: The woman asks to be set 'like a seal on your heart, like a seal on your arm'. A seal was a stamp carried on a cord over the heart or as a ring on the hand, a mark of ownership and a part of a person's identity (Genesis 38:18; Jeremiah 22:24). The high priest carried the tribes' names on his heart (Exodus 28:29). Christian readers have joined the verse to the Spirit's seal on believers (2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13), a different image.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 8:6; Genesis 38:18; Jeremiah 22:24; Exodus 28:29; 2 Corinthians 1:22; Ephesians 1:13

sections.h: The Song at Passover
sections.b: Jewish custom reads the Song in the synagogue on the Sabbath of Passover week. The reasons are the spring setting of 2:8–14 and the reading of the Song as the story of God's love for Israel from the Exodus on. Song of Songs Rabbah ties 2:8–9 to the exodus from Egypt. The custom of reading the Song at Passover is first described in the minor tractate Soferim (chapter 14), usually dated to about the eighth century.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 2:8–14; Exodus 12:1–14

sections.h: The four praise-songs and the lovers' speeches
sections.b: The Song's four wasf poems (4:1–7; 5:10–16; 6:4–10; 7:1–9) run from the head down, the head down again, partly repeated, and from the feet up. They compare body parts to animals, plants, towers and jewels, and describe impression and not shape. The repeated lines in 4:1–3 and 6:5–7 are a main argument in the debate over whether the Song is one poem or many.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 4:1–7; Song of Songs 5:10–16; Song of Songs 6:4–10; Song of Songs 7:1–9

sections.h: Desire in the Song of Songs
sections.b: The Song gives the woman the first and the last word and many of the invitations: 'let him kiss me' (1:2), 'let my lover come into his garden' (4:16), 'there I will give you my lovemaking' (7:12). The man answers in kind. The Song speaks of breasts, thighs, hands and navels in plain words and in images, and it never blames the lovers. It also shows the cost: the second night search ends in a beating (5:7), and the oath asks the daughters not to rouse love before its time.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 1:2; Song of Songs 4:16; Song of Songs 5:7; Song of Songs 7:12; Song of Songs 8:4

sections.h: The spices of the Song
sections.b: The Song names nard (1:12; 4:13–14), myrrh (1:13; 3:6; 4:6, 14; 5:1, 5, 13), henna (1:14; 4:13), saffron, calamus and cinnamon (4:14), frankincense (3:6; 4:6, 14), aloes (4:14) and 'spices' (4:10, 14, 16; 5:1, 13; 6:2; 8:14). Most were imported from Arabia, India and beyond, and nard, cinnamon, aloes, frankincense and myrrh could not grow in an Israelite garden (henna did, at En-gedi, 1:14); the garden of 4:12–15 is a poem of wealth and desire, not a plant list.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 1:12–14; Song of Songs 3:6; Song of Songs 4:6; Song of Songs 4:13–14; Song of Songs 5:1; Song of Songs 5:5; Song of Songs 8:14

sections.h: The Shulammite in the Song
sections.b: The name appears only in 6:13, where the chorus asks her to come back so they may look at her, and she asks why they look at her as they would at the dance of the two camps. The Greek and Latin read Shunammite. Views differ on whether she is the woman of the whole Song, a stock name for the bride, or a woman of the court. The sound of the name is close to Shelomoh, Solomon, and to shalom, peace.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 6:13; Song of Songs 7:1; Song of Songs 8:10

sections.h: How the Song was read allegorically
sections.b: The Targum reads the Song as the history of Israel from the Exodus to the end of days, with God as the lover. Song of Songs Rabbah and Rashi follow this line. Origen, Gregory of Nyssa, Ambrose, Bernard, Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross read it as the soul or the Church and Christ. The reading has two strengths its defenders name: it explains why a book without God's name was kept, and it fits the prophets' language of marriage between God and his people. Its critics say it overlooks the poem's plain subject.
sections.refs: Song of Songs 1:2; Song of Songs 2:8–14; Song of Songs 4:12; Song of Songs 8:6–7
